1040: Think of "arrive at" as meaning to reach something — either a place or an answer. That's the heart of it. The phrase works in two big ways: in the real, physical world and in the world of thinking.
Meaning 1: To Reach a Physical Place

When you travel somewhere and you get there, you arrive at that place.

Examples:

  • We arrived at the hotel just before midnight.
  • She arrived at the bus stop too late and missed it.
  • The guests arrived at the wedding hall by 5 PM.

This is straightforward. You were somewhere else. You traveled. You got there. You arrived at it.
Meaning 2: To Reach a Conclusion, Decision, or Answer (Through Thinking)

This is the more important and widely used meaning. When you think deeply about a problem, discuss something with others, or study a situation carefully — and then finally reach an answer or a decision — you arrive at that conclusion or decision.

The idea is that your mind goes on a journey, just like your body does when you travel. Thinking is the road. The conclusion is the destination. When you finally get there, you have arrived at it.

Examples:

  • After hours of discussion, the committee arrived at a decision.
  • How did you arrive at that conclusion?
  • Scientists arrived at this result after years of research.
  • The two countries finally arrived at an agreement.
  • I sat with the problem for weeks before I arrived at a solution.

Notice that in every case, there is a process happening before the arrival. You don't just suddenly have an answer — you work toward it, think through it, or discuss it, and then you arrive at it. This sense of effort and journey is baked into the phrase.
"Arrive At" vs. "Arrive In" — A Key Distinction

This is one of the most important things to know, and many learners get confused here.

Use "arrive at" for specific, smaller locations — a building, a venue, an event, a place with a clear boundary.

  • arrive at the airport
  • arrive at school
  • arrive at the station
  • arrive at the conference
  • arrive at someone's house

Use "arrive in" for large areas — cities, countries, regions, or continents.

  • arrive in London
  • arrive in Japan
  • arrive in Europe
  • arrive in the north

Special case — "arrive home": When you arrive home, you use no preposition at all. You don't say "arrive at home." You simply say "I arrived home."

A simple way to remember this:

Small and specific = "at." Large and broad = "in." Home = nothing.
The Words That Most Commonly Go With "Arrive At" (Collocations)

In the figurative sense, "arrive at" is almost always followed by one of these words. Learning these combinations will make you sound natural:

  • Arrive at a conclusion — after thinking something through
  • Arrive at a decision — after weighing options
  • Arrive at an agreement — after negotiating
  • Arrive at a solution — after working on a problem
  • Arrive at an answer — after figuring something out
  • Arrive at a consensus — after a group discusses and agrees
  • Arrive at an understanding — after clearing up confusion between people
  • Arrive at a verdict — what a jury does at the end of a trial

These are the natural partners of "arrive at." When you see or hear this phrase, it will almost certainly be followed by one of these words.

You might wonder: can't you just say "reach a conclusion" instead of "arrive at a conclusion"? Yes, you can — they mean the same thing. But "arrive at" carries a slightly stronger sense of process and effort. It emphasizes that you traveled mentally or physically to get there. "Reach" is more neutral. In formal writing and speech, "arrive at" is very commonly preferred.
Register: When and Where Is This Phrase Used?

• In everyday speech, the literal meaning (arriving at places) is completely normal and casual.
  • The figurative meaning tends to be slightly more formal. You'll see it often in academic writing, news articles, business discussions, legal settings, and scientific papers. However, it also appears in everyday conversation without sounding stiff.

Mistake 1: Saying "arrive at" when you should say "arrive in."

❌ We arrived at France.
✅ We arrived in France.

Mistake 2: Saying "arrive to."

❌ She arrived to the station.
✅ She arrived at the station.

"Arrive to" is a very common error among learners. English does not use "to" after "arrive." Always use "at" or "in" depending on the size of the place.

Mistake 3: Saying "arrive at home."

❌ I arrived at home.
✅ I arrived home.

"Arrive at" is a phrase built on one powerful image: reaching a destination. Whether that destination is a building you walked into or a conclusion you thought your way into, the phrase captures the same thing — the end of a journey. In the physical world, you arrive at places. In the world of the mind, you arrive at answers, decisions, and agreements — but only after a real process of working through things.

Master this phrase and you will handle it correctly in both casual conversation and formal writing.
1041: An arriviste is a person who claws their way to the top of society or their profession with naked, shameless ambition — often by being fake, manipulative, or ruthless — and who others look down on for it, even when they succeed.

An arriviste is not simply an ambitious person. Ambition alone is neutral, even admirable. What makes someone an arriviste is the how — the way they pursue success with a kind of desperate, undignified hunger that involves cutting ethical corners, pretending to be someone they're not, flattering people they privately despise, and stepping on whoever gets in their way.

The word is always an insult. When you call someone an arriviste, you are being contemptuous. You are saying: "I can see exactly what you're doing, and it's ugly."

Picture this kind of person in action:

They shower powerful people with flattery, not because they genuinely admire them, but because those people can be useful. They present a polished, carefully constructed version of themselves — borrowing tastes, opinions, and manners from whatever world they're trying to break into — while hiding who they really are and where they really came from. They drop people the moment those people stop being useful. They take credit for others' work. They betray allies when it's convenient. And through all of this, they keep a smile on their face.

There is a deep phoniness at the heart of the arriviste. Everything they do is calculated. Every friendship is an investment. Every relationship is a rung on the ladder.

The word carries a strong sense of someone being an outsider forcing their way in. Historically, and even in how it's used today, the arriviste is often someone from a humble or unremarkable background trying to penetrate a world — high society, elite intellectual circles, powerful institutions — that has its own unspoken rules and codes. They don't naturally belong, and their effort to fit in is seen as strained, obvious, and a little embarrassing by those already on the inside.

This doesn't mean arrivistes always fail. They often succeed spectacularly. But they are never quite respected. The people around them can smell the calculation. There's a quiet contempt directed at them, even from those who shake their hand and smile.
How it's different from similar words

Lots of words describe ambitious or self-serving people, but "arriviste" is sharper and more specific than most:

A social climber is the closest everyday equivalent — someone trying to move up in status. But "arriviste" is more cutting, more literary, and implies a greater degree of moral compromise and fakeness.

An opportunist takes advantage of situations when they arise. That's more neutral — it doesn't necessarily imply the relentless, desperate quality of the arriviste.

A careerist focuses heavily on advancing professionally, but the word doesn't carry the same sense of ruthlessness or social fakery.

"Arriviste" combines all the worst elements: the social climbing, the manipulation, the phoniness, the ruthlessness, and the quiet desperation underneath it all. It is the most precise and most damning of the group.
The tone and register of the word

This is a sophisticated, literary word. You're more likely to encounter it in a sharp essay, a quality novel, or serious journalism than in everyday conversation. When a writer reaches for "arriviste," they're making a precise, carefully aimed attack on someone's character — not a vague accusation, but a specific portrait of a certain type of person.

Using this word well signals that you're making a refined, exact judgment. It's not casual slang. It has an air of cool, almost aristocratic disdain.
Sentences that show the word in use

• "The new editor was a brilliant arriviste — charming at dinner parties, merciless in the office, and loyal to absolutely no one."
  • "She had always been an arriviste, collecting powerful friends the way others collect insurance policies."
  • "His colleagues respected his results but despised him personally; they saw him for the arriviste he was."
The one-line summary to remember forever

An arriviste is someone who will do whatever it takes — lie, flatter, fake, and betray — to reach the top, and whom everyone around them privately sees through and looks down on, regardless of whether they succeed.
1042:
Arrogance is the attitude of a person who believes they are far more important, more capable, or more valuable than they actually are — and who shows this belief in a way that is offensive or dismissive to others.

Think of it this way: arrogance is not just thinking you are great. It is thinking you are so great that other people barely matter in comparison.

At the heart of arrogance are two things happening at once:

1. An inflated sense of self
An arrogant person has an exaggerated opinion of their own worth — their intelligence, status, talent, beauty, power, or importance. This opinion is usually not fully deserved, or at least not as fully deserved as they believe.

2. A dismissive attitude toward others
Because they place themselves so high, they naturally place others lower. They look down on people, treat others as inferior, and act as though the feelings, opinions, or needs of others are less important than their own.

These two things feed each other. The more a person inflates themselves, the more they shrink everyone else.
What Arrogance Looks Like in Real Life

Arrogance is not an invisible feeling — it shows. Here are the most common ways it appears in behaviour:

  • Interrupting others because they assume their point is more valuable.
  • Refusing to listen to advice, feedback, or criticism, even when it is correct and helpful.
  • Talking down to people — using a tone or language that makes the other person feel small or stupid.
  • Never admitting mistakes, because admitting a mistake would mean they are not as perfect as they believe.
  • Taking credit for shared success and giving little or no acknowledgment to others.
  • Boasting and bragging repeatedly, even when no one asked.
  • Treating rules as things that apply to other people, but not to them.
  • Expecting special treatment — being served first, listened to first, or prioritised, simply because of who they think they are.

Imagine a student who scores 80% on a test. Two reactions are possible:

Reaction A (Confident): "I did well! I'm proud of my effort, and I'll keep working hard."

Reaction B (Arrogant): "I'm obviously the most talented person in this class. The teacher's questions were poorly written anyway, and the others just aren't on my level."

Reaction B is arrogance. Notice that the arrogant person:

  • Assumes their result makes them superior to others
  • Refuses to accept any flaw (blames the teacher instead)
  • Dismisses everyone else without a fair assessment
Arrogance vs. Confidence — A Critical Difference

This is one of the most important distinctions to understand, because many people confuse the two.

Confidence says: "I believe in my abilities."
Arrogance says: "My abilities make me better than you."

A confident person can say "I'm good at this" without needing to add "...and you're not." They respect others even while respecting themselves. They can accept being wrong. They don't need to put others down to feel good about themselves.

An arrogant person, on the other hand, needs to feel above others. Their sense of self-worth depends on the comparison. They feel tall only by making others feel small.

In short: confidence is self-assurance. Arrogance is self-assurance at someone else's expense.
Arrogance vs. Pride — Another Important Distinction

Pride (in its healthy form) is a quiet satisfaction in your achievements or qualities. It is self-directed and proportionate.

Arrogance is pride that has grown out of control and turned outward — it demands that others recognize and submit to your superiority. It is also disproportionate: the belief in one's own greatness exceeds what is actually warranted.

You can be proud of your work without being arrogant. But arrogance almost always involves a distorted, exaggerated kind of pride.
Why Is Arrogance Considered a Negative Quality?

Arrogance is widely seen as a flaw for several strong reasons:

  • It damages relationships. People do not enjoy being around someone who makes them feel inferior or ignored.
  • It blocks growth. An arrogant person cannot learn from mistakes, accept good advice, or improve — because in their mind, they are already perfect enough.
  • It is often inaccurate. Arrogance frequently involves a wrong self-assessment. The person overestimates themselves.
  • It is disrespectful. Arrogance disrespects the dignity and worth of other people.
  • It creates conflict. Arrogant behaviour provokes resentment, arguments, and broken trust.
How the Word Is Used in Sentences

• "His arrogance made it impossible for anyone on the team to offer suggestions."
  • "She walked into the meeting with such arrogance that she didn't bother learning anyone's name."
  • "The arrogance of that leader eventually caused his downfall — he ignored all warnings."
  • "There is a fine line between confidence and arrogance, and he crossed it long ago."
Arrogance is the attitude of someone who thinks too highly of themselves and too little of others — and shows it.
1043:
When someone is arrogant, they believe they are better, more important, or more capable than other people — and they show this belief through how they behave. It's not just a private feeling; it comes out in the way they treat others.

An arrogant person has an exaggerated, inflated opinion of themselves. They think too highly of their own intelligence, abilities, status, or worth. And because of this, they look down on others, often without even realizing it.
The key thing that makes it arrogance

Here's something important to understand: simply thinking well of yourself is not arrogance. What turns it into arrogance is how you treat other people as a result.

An arrogant person acts as though other people are beneath them — less smart, less important, less worthy of respect. That dismissiveness toward others is the heart of arrogance.
What arrogant behavior looks like in real life

If someone is arrogant, you'll often notice patterns like these:

  • They rarely say "I was wrong" or apologize, even when they clearly made a mistake
  • They don't genuinely listen to others — they just wait for their turn to talk
  • They dismiss other people's ideas or opinions without seriously considering them
  • They interrupt or talk over others
  • They expect special treatment or to be taken more seriously than everyone else
  • They speak with great certainty even when they don't actually know what they're talking about
  • They take credit easily but rarely give it to others
  • They react badly to criticism — often getting defensive, angry, or dismissive
How it feels to be around an arrogant person

Spending time with an arrogant person is often unpleasant. You tend to feel:

  • Dismissed — like your opinion doesn't count
  • Disrespected — like you're not being treated as an equal
  • Talked down to — like they're speaking to someone beneath them
  • Unheard — like nothing you say really lands with them

This is a useful test: if someone consistently makes the people around them feel small or unimportant, arrogance is likely part of the picture.
Arrogant vs. similar words (important distinctions)
These words are often confused, so understanding the differences will sharpen your understanding of arrogant specifically.
Arrogant vs. Confident

This is the most important distinction. A confident person believes in themselves — but they still respect others, listen to feedback, and acknowledge their limits. An arrogant person doesn't just believe in themselves; they believe they are superior to others, and it shows in how they treat people. Confidence is self-assured. Arrogance is self-superior.

Think of it this way: a confident surgeon says, "I've trained hard and I'm good at what I do." An arrogant surgeon says (in tone or action), "I don't need to hear your concerns, I know better than you."
Arrogant vs. Proud

You can be proud of something in a healthy, grounded way — proud of your work, your team, your growth. Arrogance is what happens when pride becomes so inflated and so focused on superiority over others that it starts coming out as disrespect or dismissiveness. Healthy pride lifts you up. Arrogance pushes others down.
Arrogant vs. Conceited

These are close cousins. Conceited leans more toward being excessively vain — being obsessed with your own looks, talents, or qualities, and fishing for admiration. Arrogant is broader and more about a sense of superiority and the dismissive treatment that follows. An arrogant person might not even care about admiration — they simply act as if they're on a higher level than others.
Arrogant vs. Haughty

Haughty means almost the same thing as arrogant but tends to suggest a cold, distant, "I am far above you" kind of superiority. Think of someone who looks down at others with a cold stare, as if they can't be bothered to engage. Haughty is arrogance with a chilly, distant quality to it.
Arrogant vs. Self-important

A self-important person takes themselves too seriously and expects others to treat them as highly significant. There's overlap with arrogant, but self-importance focuses more on demanding status and seriousness, while arrogance focuses more on the feeling of being better than others.
Arrogance exists on a spectrum

Not all arrogance looks the same. Someone can be mildly arrogant — slightly dismissive of others' opinions, a little too sure of themselves — or deeply arrogant — openly contemptuous, condescending in almost every interaction. The word covers the full range.
A subtle but important nuance

Arrogance is sometimes a mask. Some people who feel deeply insecure on the inside put on an arrogant front to protect themselves — to avoid looking weak, or to control how others see them. So beneath the arrogance, there might be fear or insecurity. This doesn't make the arrogant behavior any less hurtful to others, but it does explain why arrogant people sometimes seem more fragile than they appear.
Example sentences

• He was so arrogant that he never once asked his team for their opinions — he assumed he already had all the answers.
  • Her arrogant tone during the meeting made everyone feel like their contributions didn't matter.
  • Despite being talented, he was difficult to work with because of his arrogant attitude — he never admitted when he was wrong.
  • The interviewer came across as arrogant, barely listening to the candidate's answers before talking over them.
  • She wasn't arrogant about her success; she was genuinely grateful and humble about how much help she had received.
One-line summary to lock it in
An arrogant person has an inflated sense of their own worth or importance — and this shows up in how they treat others: dismissively, condescendingly, or as if other people simply don't measure up.
1044:
To arrogate means to claim or take a right, power, or privilege for yourself — when you have absolutely no legitimate basis to do so. The defining element is wrongful presumption: you are helping yourself to something that isn't yours to take, and you are doing so with a kind of boldness, as if you were entitled to it.

The most common phrasing you'll encounter is "arrogate to oneself" — meaning a person presumptuously seizes something for themselves. Keep this phrase in mind; it is the heartbeat of the word.

Imagine a junior employee at a company who, with no authority whatsoever, begins making decisions reserved for the CEO — firing staff, changing company policy, signing major contracts. Nobody appointed him. Nobody asked him. He just did it, as if those powers were his to take. That employee is arrogating to himself authority that belongs to someone else.

The person arrogating something usually knows — or certainly should know — that they have no right to it. There is always a sense of overstepping, of crossing a line that was clearly drawn.
What Kinds of Things Get Arrogated?

This is important: arrogate is almost always used for abstract things, not physical objects. You would never say "he arrogated my bicycle." The word lives squarely in the world of power, authority, rights, titles, and privileges. A general arrogates military command. A government arrogates the right to imprison people without trial. A committee member arrogates the authority to speak on behalf of the whole group. These are the natural territories of this word.

Arrogate carries a strong negative tone. It doesn't just mean that someone is taking something wrongfully — it implies they are doing so with audacity and a sense of entitlement. The underlying question arrogate always raises is: "Who gave you the right to do that?"

This is what sharply separates arrogate from a neutral word like "claim." You can legitimately claim something — a claim can be valid or invalid. But when you arrogate something, it is by definition always wrongful. The illegitimacy is baked directly into the word. There is no such thing as a justified act of arrogation.

The general arrogated to himself the power to declare war, completely bypassing parliament.

She arrogated the right to make decisions for the entire team without consulting a single person.

The new governor arrogated powers that the constitution had carefully reserved for the judiciary.

No individual can arrogate to themselves the authority to speak on behalf of an entire nation.

Notice the consistent thread: someone reaches into a space of authority or rights that was never theirs, and takes from it as if it were.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Usurp is the closest cousin. Both involve seizing power wrongfully. However, usurp tends to be reserved for larger, more dramatic takeovers — seizing a throne, overthrowing a government. Arrogate is broader and applies equally well to smaller, everyday overreaches of authority, like a manager making decisions above his rank.

Assume can also mean to take on a role, but it is neutral or even positive — a new president assumes office, a doctor assumes responsibility for a patient. Arrogate has no neutral use; it is always an indictment.

Appropriate (in its verb form) can mean to take something for yourself, but again it is more neutral. Arrogate always carries the sting of presumption and wrongfulness.

Arrogate typically appears in one of two constructions. The first — and more classic — is arrogate to oneself: "He arrogated to himself the right to decide." The second simply pairs arrogate directly with what is being taken: "She arrogated that authority." Both are correct, but the first form is more elegant and far more common in formal writing.
Register: Where You'll Meet This Word

Arrogate is a formal word. You will find it in legal writing, political commentary, philosophy, history, and serious journalism. It is the language of scholars, judges, and critics describing an overreach of authority. You are unlikely to hear it in everyday conversation, and that's okay — knowing it equips you to understand and use it precisely when it matters.

Arrogation is the noun form — the act of arrogating. For example: "The arrogation of judicial power by the executive branch alarmed legal scholars." Arrogator is the rare noun for a person who arrogates, though you'll seldom encounter it.
To arrogate is to presumptuously claim or seize a right, power, or authority for yourself — when you have no legitimate right to it whatsoever.
1045:
An arroyo is a dry, channel-like ditch or gully carved into the ground by water — but here's the key: it holds little or no water most of the time. It only fills up temporarily when heavy rain hits.

Think of it as a stream that forgot to bring its water permanently. The channel is there. The flowing water is not — except when it rains hard.

Picture a narrow, trench-like channel cut into dry, dusty earth. Its sides are steep or sloping, like the walls of a small canyon. The bottom is flat or slightly curved. It may be anywhere from a few feet wide to dozens of feet wide. Loose sand, gravel, and rocks often line the floor. There are no fish, no reeds, no signs of a living stream — just a bare, empty groove in the ground baking in the sun.

Arroyos are characteristic of arid (very dry) and semi-arid regions — places that don't get much rain. The American Southwest is the classic location: Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, Nevada, Colorado, and across the border in Mexico. You'll also encounter the word in descriptions of similar landscapes in South America, Africa, and parts of Central Asia.

In these regions, rain doesn't fall gently and steadily. Instead, it comes in sudden, intense bursts — and then nothing for weeks or months.
How an Arroyo Forms and Why It's Dry

In dry landscapes, the ground is hard and often can't absorb rain quickly. When a sudden rainstorm hits, water rushes over the surface, gathers into a torrent, and cuts through the soft or cracked earth, carving out a channel. This happens over many storms across many years.

But between rainstorms, there's no steady source of water — no snowmelt feeding it, no underground spring keeping it alive. So the channel sits empty, baking under the sun.

This is the most important thing to understand about an arroyo in practical terms. Even though an arroyo looks perfectly dry and harmless — you could walk across the flat sandy bottom without getting your feet wet — it can transform into a deadly, roaring torrent within minutes.

Here's why: a thunderstorm may be happening many miles upstream, far out of sight. You may be standing in the arroyo under a clear sky, completely unaware. That distant rain sends a wall of fast-moving water rushing down the channel toward you. Because the walls are steep, there's often nowhere to climb quickly. This is why warning signs near arroyos say things like "Do not enter when flooded" — and hikers and drivers are strongly cautioned never to enter or cross an arroyo during or after rain anywhere in the region.

This sudden, violent filling is called a flash flood, and arroyos are one of the most common places where flash flood deaths occur.

You may encounter other words that describe similar features. Here's how to distinguish them:

  • Creek / stream / river — these have flowing water most or all of the time. An arroyo normally does not.
  • Wash / dry wash — essentially the same thing as an arroyo. "Wash" is just the more common everyday term in parts of the American West (especially Arizona). Arroyo tends to be more formal or literary.
  • Gulch — similar, but gulch usually implies a deeper, narrower cut and is more associated with mountainous terrain. Arroyos are more specific to flat desert and semi-arid plains.
  • Ravine — a ravine is a narrow valley or gorge, and it can be in any climate, not necessarily dry land. An arroyo is specifically tied to dry, arid environments.
  • Gully — a smaller, shallower erosion channel. An arroyo is typically larger and more established. All arroyos could loosely be called gullies, but not all gullies are arroyos.

• "We camped near the arroyo, but we made sure to set up on the high bank in case of rain."
  • "The hiking trail crossed three arroyos before reaching the canyon rim."
  • "After the storm, the usually silent arroyo became a brown, churning river."
  • "The old ranch house was built just above an arroyo that flooded every monsoon season."
An arroyo is a steep-sided, normally dry channel or gully in arid land, carved by water over time, which fills suddenly and dangerously with rushing water during and after heavy rain.
1046:
Arsenal means a large stock of weapons and military equipment — either the place where they are stored or made, or the collection of weapons itself.

Think of it as a "weapon warehouse." A country or an army doesn't keep just one gun or one missile — they keep thousands of them, all organized and ready to use. That entire supply, or the facility that holds it, is called an arsenal.

The word carries two closely related literal meanings, and both are correct:

1. A place (a building or facility)
This is a physical location — a large government-run building or complex — where weapons are manufactured, stored, repaired, or distributed. Armies and governments maintain these places so that their military forces always have weapons ready when needed.

"The soldiers retrieved their equipment from the national arsenal before heading to the border."

2. A collection of weapons
Here, "arsenal" doesn't refer to a place at all — it refers to the weapons themselves as a group. When a country is said to have a "nuclear arsenal," it means the total number of nuclear weapons that country possesses and could use.

"The country's arsenal included hundreds of warships, fighter jets, and missiles."
The Figurative Meaning (Very Common in Everyday Language)

This is where the word gets very interesting and widely used. Over time, people began using "arsenal" to talk about things that have nothing to do with weapons at all.

Figuratively, an arsenal means any large, powerful collection of tools, skills, resources, or techniques that a person or group can draw upon to achieve something.

The logic is simple: just as an army draws on its arsenal of weapons to win a battle, a person draws on their "arsenal" of skills or resources to succeed at something.

Here are some examples:

  • A doctor has an arsenal of treatments — meaning a wide variety of medicines, procedures, and therapies they can use to fight a disease.
  • A lawyer walks into court with an arsenal of arguments — meaning many strong, well-prepared points ready to be used.
  • A chef has an arsenal of techniques — meaning a deep, impressive set of cooking skills they can apply.
  • A teacher has an arsenal of methods to explain a difficult topic — meaning many different approaches they can try.

In every case, the figurative meaning carries the same feeling: a large, powerful, ready-to-use collection of something that gives you an advantage.
What Makes "Arsenal" Special — The Exact Feeling It Carries

It is worth understanding why someone would choose the word "arsenal" over a simpler word like "collection" or "set." The difference is in the feeling it carries.

"Arsenal" is not a neutral word. It always implies:

  • Abundance — not just a few things, but many.
  • Power — these are not ordinary resources; they are strong, effective ones.
  • Readiness — everything is organized and prepared to be used at a moment's notice.
  • Strategic advantage — having a large arsenal means you are well-equipped to handle challenges.

So when someone says a tennis player has "an impressive arsenal of shots," they are saying that player has many different shots, all of them strong, and they can pull any one of them out whenever the match demands it. That is a much richer and more vivid idea than simply saying the player has "many shots."

Arsenal is usually used with positive or neutral intent. When used figuratively, saying someone has "a vast arsenal" of skills is almost always a compliment. It means they are formidable, well-prepared, and capable.

The size matters. You would not call two or three things an "arsenal." The word inherently suggests a large supply. It would sound odd or exaggerated to say "she had an arsenal of two ideas." The word works best when the quantity or quality is genuinely impressive.

It is most commonly used with these kinds of words:

  • nuclear arsenal, military arsenal (literal)
  • vast arsenal, impressive arsenal, extensive arsenal, growing arsenal (figurative emphasis on size)
  • arsenal of weapons, arsenal of tools, arsenal of skills, arsenal of options (figurative categories)

ContextWhat "arsenal" means
  • Literally: A place where weapons are stored/made, OR the entire collection of weapons a military force possesses.
  • Figuratively: Any large, powerful, ready-to-use collection of skills, tools, techniques, or resources that gives someone a strong advantage.

The word always carries a sense of abundance, power, and readiness. Whether someone is talking about a country's missiles or a writer's vocabulary, calling it an "arsenal" tells you it is large, impressive, and purposefully built to win.
1047:
Arson is the crime of deliberately setting fire to property — such as a building, vehicle, forest, or any other structure — with the intent to destroy or damage it. The single most important word in understanding arson is deliberately. The fire must be set on purpose. If a fire breaks out accidentally — say, from a fallen candle, a lightning strike, or a faulty wire — that is not arson, no matter how much destruction it causes.

Arson is always a crime. It is one of the most serious offenses in virtually every legal system in the world.
The Three Core Elements of Arson

For a fire to legally qualify as arson, three things must be true:

  1. A fire was set (or attempted). An actual fire must occur. In many legal systems, even attempting to set a fire — and failing — can still be charged as attempted arson.
  2. It was done intentionally. The person knew what they were doing and chose to do it. There was a conscious decision to start the fire.
  3. It involved property. The fire targets something that belongs to someone — a building, a car, land, or goods.

All three elements must be present. Remove the intention, and it's an accident. Remove the property, and there's no target to speak of.
A Very Important Misconception: You Can Commit Arson on Your OWN Property

Many people assume arson only means burning someone else's property. This is wrong. If you deliberately set fire to your own home, your own car, or your own business — that is still arson. The law does not care who owns the property. Why? Because fire is wildly unpredictable. Your burning house can spread to your neighbor's house. Your burning car can endanger lives on a street. The crime is about the deliberate, dangerous act, not just whose name is on the property deed.

This is why arson for insurance fraud — burning your own property to collect insurance money — is one of the most common forms of arson.

People commit arson for a variety of reasons:

  • Insurance fraud — The most common motive. A person burns down their own home, business, or vehicle so they can claim the insurance payout. For example, a struggling business owner burning their shop to get the insurance money.
  • Revenge or hatred — Setting fire to an enemy's property out of anger, spite, or jealousy.
  • Concealing another crime — Burning a crime scene to destroy evidence like fingerprints, blood, or bodies. This is sometimes done to cover up a murder.
  • Vandalism — Mindless, destructive behavior, often with no specific motive other than causing chaos.
  • Terrorism or intimidation — Fires used as a weapon to terrorize communities or send a threatening message.
  • Pyromania — A rare but real psychological condition where a person has an uncontrollable, compulsive urge to set fires and is dangerously fascinated by them. A pyromaniac may not have a practical motive — they simply cannot resist the impulse.
Degrees of Arson (How Serious It Is)

Most legal systems recognize that not all arson is equally dangerous, so they classify it into degrees:

  • First-degree arson — Setting fire to an occupied building where people are present. This is the most severe form because it directly endangers human lives.
  • Second-degree arson — Setting fire to an unoccupied building.
  • Third-degree arson — Setting fire to abandoned or derelict property.

The higher the degree, the harsher the punishment.
Why the Law Takes Arson So Seriously

Arson is treated as a grave crime — typically a felony — for these reasons:

  • Fire is completely unpredictable once it starts. It can spread instantly beyond the intended target, killing bystanders, neighbors, and even firefighters.
  • It causes enormous financial damage not just to the direct victim, but to entire communities.
  • It is difficult to control and nearly impossible to undo once it begins.
  • It is often used to cover up even worse crimes.

The penalties for arson are severe:

  • Prison sentences, which can range from several years to life imprisonment in the most extreme cases.
  • Heavy fines.
  • A permanent criminal record.
  • If someone dies as a result of the fire — even unintentionally — the arsonist can additionally be charged with murder or manslaughter on top of the arson charge.

Specially trained professionals called arson investigators (or fire investigators) examine fire scenes to determine whether a fire was accidental or deliberately set. They look for clues like the fire's point of origin, the pattern of burn marks, the presence of accelerants (flammable liquids like gasoline used to help the fire spread faster), and other physical evidence. Interestingly, many arsonists are known to return to the scene of the fire to watch it burn — and this behavior has actually led to the arrest of many of them.

Here are some example sentences showing how "arson" is used:

  • "Police are investigating the warehouse fire as a case of arson."
  • "She was sentenced to eight years in prison for arson after setting fire to her former employer's office."
  • "The insurance company refused to pay the claim when investigators discovered the fire was caused by arson."
  • "Arson destroyed three homes before firefighters could control the blaze."

Arson is the deliberate, intentional crime of setting fire to property — whether your own or someone else's — and it is a serious felony because fire endangers lives and can cause catastrophic, irreversible destruction.

An artery is a tube-like blood vessel — a hollow channel inside your body — that carries blood away from the heart and delivers it to the rest of the body. That single direction (away from the heart) is the defining feature of every artery.

Think of your heart as a pump. Every time it beats, it pushes blood outward with great force. Arteries are the pipes that receive that forceful surge and distribute blood to every organ, muscle, and tissue — your brain, lungs, arms, legs, and everything in between.

Your body has three types of blood vessels: arteries, veins, and capillaries. Arteries and veins are commonly mixed up, so here is a clean distinction:

  • Arteries carry blood away from the heart.
  • Veins carry blood back toward the heart.
  • Capillaries are the tiny connecting vessels in between, where oxygen and nutrients are actually handed off to individual cells.

A memory trick: Artery → Away.

Arteries have thick, muscular, and elastic walls. This is because blood inside them is under high pressure — the direct force of each heartbeat. That pressure is also why you can feel a pulse in certain arteries (like the one in your wrist or neck): you're feeling the rhythmic surge each time the heart beats. Veins, by contrast, have thinner walls because blood travels through them at much lower pressure.
Do arteries always carry oxygenated blood?

A common shortcut taught in schools is: "Arteries carry oxygen-rich blood; veins carry oxygen-poor blood." This is mostly true but not always — and the exception matters.

The pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood from the heart to the lungs, where the blood picks up fresh oxygen. They are still arteries — they still carry blood away from the heart — but their blood is not oxygenated. So the true definition of an artery is about direction, not oxygen content.

After the lungs re-oxygenate the blood, it returns to the heart via the pulmonary veins, and the heart then pumps it out through the systemic arteries to the rest of the body. This is the complete circulatory loop.
Key arteries in the human body

The largest and most important artery is the aorta. It rises directly out of the heart and arches downward, branching out like a tree into progressively smaller arteries throughout the body. These smaller arteries branch further into even tinier vessels called arterioles, and those connect to capillaries.

Some other well-known arteries:

  • Coronary arteries — supply blood to the heart muscle itself. A blockage here is what causes a heart attack.
  • Carotid arteries — run up the neck and supply blood to the brain. A blockage here can cause a stroke.
  • Radial artery — runs along your inner wrist. This is what a doctor or nurse presses when they check your pulse manually.
  • Femoral artery — the main artery of the thigh, often used in medical procedures.
  • Pulmonary arteries — the exception discussed above; carry deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

Arteries can become diseased. The most common condition is atherosclerosis — a gradual buildup of fatty deposits (called plaque) on the inner walls of an artery. This narrows the passage, restricts blood flow, and can eventually trigger a heart attack or stroke. High blood pressure (hypertension) is also closely tied to artery health, because constantly elevated pressure damages artery walls over time.

Because arteries carry blood under high pressure, a rupture or deep cut to an artery is a medical emergency — blood escapes rapidly and in large volume. This is why arterial bleeding looks different from ordinary bleeding: it often spurts in rhythm with the heartbeat.
The figurative meaning: a major route or channel

Outside of medicine, "artery" is used to describe any major route or channel through which traffic, people, goods, or information flow. Just as a blood artery carries vital flow through a body, a figurative artery carries vital flow through a city, region, or system.

Examples in use:

  • "The motorway is a main artery connecting the two cities."
  • "The river was once the economic artery of the entire region."
  • "The blocked artery of traffic caused chaos in the city centre."

You'll also hear the adjective form arterial — as in arterial road (a major road) or arterial network (a system of main routes). This figurative use is very common in urban planning, geography, transport journalism, and everyday conversation.

SenseMeaning

In its primary sense, an artery is a blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart, with thick walls designed to handle high pressure. In its extended sense, it means any major channel — road, river, or route — through which something vital flows. The two senses share the same core idea: an artery is not a minor path; it is a main channel that keeps a system alive.
1049: Artesian describes underground water that is naturally trapped under pressure, causing it to rise on its own — sometimes all the way to the surface — when a well is drilled or a crack opens.
The Core Idea: Pressurized, Self-Rising Water

To understand "artesian," you need to understand one key fact about how some underground water works.

Normally, when you dig a well, you're reaching water that just sits in the ground. To get it out, you need a pump. But in certain geological conditions, underground water is under natural pressure — and when you tap into it, it pushes itself upward, the way water shoots out of a squeezed bottle.

That pressurized state is what makes something "artesian."
Why Does the Water Have Pressure?

Here's how artesian pressure builds up:

  1. There's a sloped landscape. Rain falls and soaks into the ground in a high area — say, a mountain or a hill. That water seeps deep into a porous rock layer (like sandstone), which can hold water the way a sponge does.
  2. The water gets trapped. Above and below this water-holding rock layer, there are layers of impermeable rock — rock that water cannot pass through (like clay or shale). The water is sandwiched and sealed in. It has nowhere to go.
  3. Gravity does the work. Because the place where water originally soaked in (the "recharge zone") is at a higher elevation than the well you drill elsewhere, gravity continuously pushes that water downhill through the rock. But since it's sealed in and can't escape, pressure builds — like squeezing a balloon from one end.
  4. You drill a hole. The moment you drill through the impermeable cap and reach the pressurized water below, that pressure has a way out. The water rushes upward.

If the pressure is high enough, water gushes right out at the surface — no pump needed. If the pressure is slightly lower, the water still rises high in the well shaft on its own, just not all the way to the top.

The adjective "artesian" is used to describe several related things:

Artesian well — This is the most common use. It's a well drilled into a pressurized underground water source. A flowing artesian well is one where the water rises and flows freely at the surface without pumping. A non-flowing artesian well is one where the water rises on its own but stops below the surface (still under pressure, just not enough to overflow). Both are "artesian" because the defining quality — natural upward pressure — is present.

Artesian spring — A natural crack or fault in the rock sometimes gives pressurized underground water a way to escape on its own, without anyone drilling. The water bursts through and flows at the surface. This is an artesian spring — nature's version of an artesian well.

Artesian aquifer — The underground layer of porous, water-holding rock that is sealed between impermeable layers and holds water under pressure. An aquifer is basically a rock layer that acts like an enormous underground water tank. When that tank is confined and pressurized, it's specifically called an artesian aquifer (or a confined aquifer).

Artesian basin — When a very large geographic region sits above an artesian aquifer, the whole region is called an artesian basin. The most famous example is the Great Artesian Basin in Australia — one of the largest underground freshwater reservoirs on Earth, stretching under parts of Queensland, New South Wales, South Australia, and the Northern Territory. It has supplied water to outback communities and livestock for over a century, often flowing to the surface on its own from wells drilled centuries ago.
The Single Quality That Makes Something "Artesian"

Whenever you see the word artesian, ask: Is the water naturally under enough pressure to rise by itself?

  • If yes → it's artesian.
  • If no → it's an ordinary (or "water-table") well or source.

The pressure is everything. That's the razor-sharp definition. A well can be deep, clean, ancient, and cold — but if the water just sits there and needs a pump, it's not artesian. A well can be relatively shallow, but if the water forces itself upward due to confined pressure, it is artesian.
A Clarification You'll Encounter on Water Bottles

You've probably seen bottled water labeled "artesian" or "artesian spring water." Technically, this should mean the water came from a confined, pressurized aquifer — a legitimate artesian source. In practice, the term is sometimes used loosely by companies to imply purity, naturalness, or depth. The true meaning, though, is always about the pressure mechanism, not just the purity.
The One Mental Image to Remember It Forever

Imagine squeezing a full, sealed water balloon from the top. Even if you poke a hole at the bottom, water shoots upward because of the pressure you're applying from above. Nature does the exact same thing: rain soaks in at high ground (squeezing from above, via gravity), seals itself between rock layers, and when you poke a hole with a drill, the water rises — or even shoots up — on its own.

That's artesian.
